newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: MD sees Asia plane growth doubling.
newsitem.headline: MD sees Asia plane growth doubling.

text.p: U.S. aircraft maker McDonnell Douglas Corp sees the growth rate for commercial aircraft sales doubling in Asia over the next 15 years, and is aiming for a greater market share, a senior company official said on Friday.

Donald Black, senior vice president of marketing and airline financing, told Reuters in an interview that he expected a resurgence in the aircraft business and "a return of optimism to the business which has been through some tough years."
"Towards 2000, we will see some substantial growth in commercial aircraft deliveries," Black said.

"We also see a substantial growth in total aircraft sales into Asia over the next 15 years," he said. "Total industry (commercial) aircraft sales into Asia over the next 15 years is projected at 4,000."
"Of these, narrow-bodied aircraft will comprise about 1,200, or $55 billion, and wide-bodied will be around 2,800, an equivalent of $390 billion," he said.
Black was in Singapore to demonstrate the twin-jet, mid-size MD-90 model, which the company touts as the world's quietist commercial airpalne.
McDonnell Douglas, Black stressed, wanted a piece of the region's growing commercial aircraft pie, and hopes to sell in Asia about half of the MD-90s it makes.
"We have 23 percent of the aircraft fleet and want to maintain that share, if not increase it," Black said. "We would like to achieve 25 percent."
A projection of Asia's potential contribution to the company's sales was unavailable.
Currently, about 80 percent of McDonnell Douglas's revenue is from military sales, while commercial sales contribute only 20 percent, Black said.

"Senior management is very supportive of the commercial aircraft industry and we are looking to expand it. We are looking to develop a new product -- the MD-95, and MD-XX, which is a major investment on our part, to continue our part in commercial business," Black said.
The company's customers in Asia include Japan Air System, Taiwan's EVA and Uni Air, and several other Chinese airlines.
Black said Tata Industries, one of India's biggest conglomerates, was still evaluating its interest in the MD-90.

"We are still talking with Tata (on selling the MD-90). We have no firm agreement of any type with Tata," Black said. "They are evaluating the airplane, but need a government approval before they can move into the airline business."

Tata's plan to set up a $400 million domestic airline in a joint venture with Singapore Airlines has been delayed more than a year pending the Indian government's decision on how much equity a foreign firm can hold.
He said McDonnell Douglas had also spoken to state-owned Indian Airlines, which flies mostly domestic routes, and Jet Airways, one of India's new private airlines.
Black said he was optimistic the MD-95 would be a good replacement for Indian Airlines's 737-200.
